title: What the River Carried
placement: Authored option. After introduction of the Burrow; no episode number or dated event adopted.
text:
Hollis had brought two cups and no repair kit. Madger noticed the missing kit before he noticed the cups.

“Something wrong with the boat?” he asked.

“Not everything I invite you to is a boat.” Hollis considered that. “This was going to be a boat. A quiet one.”

They had reached the west waiting court at Floodglass Ford when a courier came up the bank without a wagon. Mud covered her trousers to the knees. Behind her, the south reach shone between low banks; farther north, the reeds stood in a patch of darker water.

“It rolled into the crossing,” she said. “Then that thing surfaced. Now it's gone.”

An upstream curl of silt moved against the river. A slate back rose briefly below the reeds. Someone near the court lifted a pole. Someone else said that if a wyrm could take a wagon, the crossing ought to be cleared of wyrms.

Madger stepped forward. He knew the particular silence that followed a frightened crowd discovering someone willing to promise an answer.

“We'll get it back,” he said.

Hollis set down the cups. “From where?”

“The river.”

“It's a long river.”

Madger heard the familiar correction and felt himself become younger. He turned toward the ford, where a rope lay half buried in mud. Hollis caught his sleeve, not hard.

“Listen to her again.”

The courier said she had left the wagon on the western approach while checking the water. The brake had slipped. She had waded after it, heard reeds tearing, and run. Her load was flour for three kitchens. She could not afford the load, let alone the wagon.

Madger looked toward his father. Hollis had not said he could afford it either.

A bank watcher closed the ford. She marked the time on the board and left the north-bank refuge approach open. The pole stayed raised until she asked its owner what he intended to do when the animal moved toward the disturbance.

He lowered it.

Hollis unfolded his boat rule. In the mud beside the approach, he measured the space between two grooves. Then he crouched beside the rope. Madger waited for the explanation that usually came before he asked for one.

This time Hollis said, “What do you see?”

“Wheels.”

“And there?”

A narrow slash crossed the wheel grooves. Mud had curled along one edge. It ran toward the old dry channel, away from the south reach.

“A rope dragged sideways.”

“Possibly. Follow it with your eyes.”

They followed on firm western ground. The slash led to a scar on a stump, then into the abandoned channel. A wagon stood behind the low bank. A boat worker was taking a pulley off its frame.

The courier ran the last few steps and stopped before she reached her load.

“You took it.”

“I pulled it out.” The worker held up the pulley as though the object could settle the difference. “I went for a chock. By the time I came back, everyone was shouting about the animal.”

The wagon had drifted only far enough to wet one wheel before the worker caught it. The load was intact except for a split sack. He had dragged it clear along the old channel, then left it out of sight while fetching a timber block. No one had seen the whole sequence. Several had already repeated it.

The courier put a paw on the flour dust. “I thought you'd ask me to pay before I could have it.”

He looked offended. Then his expression changed. “I thought you knew it was here.”

Madger almost laughed with relief. Instead he looked back toward the raised bank. The accusation had traveled farther than the wagon.

They returned to the watcher together. Madger asked her to record what each of them had actually observed. He spoke loudly enough for the waiting court to hear.

“The wyrm didn't take this wagon. I said we'd get it back before I knew where it was. The tow marks led us here. The animal's still by the reeds, and the ford is still closed.”

“Then we wait because of a harmless animal?” someone asked.

A long slate head lifted above the water. The whiskers spread; the body turned across the reed patch. Hollis took one deliberate step back from the bank. Madger stepped with him.

“Because of an animal protecting that patch,” the watcher said. “Harmless isn't the other choice.”

The courier could recover her wagon along the western ground, but she could not cross. Her kitchens were on the other side. They arranged a message for the boat crews rather than forcing a departure before the crews had assessed the water. One kitchen would use its reserve. Another would change its meal. The third would receive less flour later. An explanation did not make a delivery arrive.

Madger helped sweep the spilled flour into a waste sack. Hollis repaired the brake stop with the courier watching, then showed her how to check it under load. By the time they finished, the tea in both cups had gone cold.

“I thought you wanted me here to tell me I was doing something wrong,” Madger said.

Hollis folded his rule carefully. “I wanted you here.”

Madger waited. His father looked at the river instead of adding anything.

They took the dry north-bank path to the refuge and sat where they could see the watchers without standing in their way. Downstream, the wyrm's back vanished. Nothing in the movement thanked them or forgave them. The reeds slowly straightened.

Hollis handed over a cup.

“Next time,” Madger said, “ask me for the quiet boat.”

“I did.”

Madger thought about that, then shifted closer so their shoulders touched. They drank the cold tea.

title: Enough of the Map
placement: Authored option. A later regional encounter; distinct from the existing Bellwater setpiece. Pending dated episode-ledger adoption.
text:
The chart Namu gave Bot ended in a clean blank margin.

Bot turned it once, checking that the fold had not hidden anything. Across the narrow strip of drawn water, soundings crowded between two rock piers. Beyond the strip, the paper showed neither shore nor settlement.

“I cannot determine whether this is incomplete,” he said.

“It is complete for the passage.”

“That is a different answer.”

Namu's rose gills stirred in the damp air. They had spent the morning explaining the same boundary to visiting traders. By noon every question sounded a little like a demand.

Then a harbor runner arrived with news of a disabled boat west of the eastern arch. Three passengers and a pilot were aboard. The hull was intact. Their small drive had stopped, and they were drifting toward the south pier.

Namu took the rescue boat's line. Bot followed with the chart, a mechanical depth line and the equipment register. He asked for the missing shoreline again.

“No,” Namu said.

Bot stopped on the quay. “I need the usable width at the pier, the depth at the landing, and a way to tell whether this chart's water level matches today's. I do not need the names of the places beyond it.”

Namu looked at the blank margin. They had drawn it as protection. They had not drawn an explanation.

“The blank is restricted shoreline, not unknown water,” they said. “I can give you those three things.”

They marked the chart with the observation time, water datum and the rescue corridor. The protected nesting pocket remained outside it. Namu kept the master chart. Bot logged the limited copy and its purpose; there would be no automatic addition to a general travel atlas.

The rescue pilot checked the boat's loading limit. There was room for the stranded passengers and their crew only if the rescue boat left its spare cargo ashore. Bot set down a sealed case of replacement fittings. He did not ask the pilot to count the case as smaller because it was important.

They left quietly. Namu stood near the bow, amber beads tucked inside their coat so they would not knock against the rail. Bot remained seated and secured; neither his body nor his tools had been assumed to tolerate an unplanned immersion.

The disabled boat slid into view beyond the southwest pier. Its pilot had kept the passengers low. A loose pump bracket tapped the hull with each small roll.

A hollow note came back from the channel.

“Bell-eel?” Bot asked.

“Possibly. Stop the tapping first.”

The stranded pilot wedged folded cloth around the bracket. Namu watched the water. A pale line passed below the surface and was gone. They did not declare the channel empty, and Bot did not turn up his optics as though brightness could drive an eel away.

A tow from the current position would bring both boats too close to the pier. Namu signaled a slow approach from the open channel. The rescue pilot held that line while the stranded crew passed a rope. No one struck the hull to hurry them.

As they drew toward the south landing, Bot lowered the weighted depth line from the stationary rescue boat. He read it, checked the reference mark and read it again.

“The landing approach is shallower than this sounding.”

Namu glanced at the cliff marks. “The water is where I expected.”

“The line reaches bottom early.”

For a moment Namu's answer was ready: the visitor was measuring a place their crews had known for generations. Then they asked him to show the reading.

Bot had measured from the rail. He corrected for the measured height of the rail above water and offered both figures, not just the alarming one. The shortfall remained. A second lowering, clear of the hull, found the same bottom.

“Deposited gravel,” Namu said. “Or a displaced stone. We cannot decide which from here.”

They marked the approach closed to the loaded rescue boat. The nearest dry refuge was plainly visible above them, but seeing it did not flatten the six metres of ascent or remove the shoal.

The stranded pilot offered to jump into the water and pull. Namu shook their head. The possibility of a bell-eel had not ceased to matter, and the current would still act on a swimmer.

Instead, the crews held both boats in the checked channel while Namu signaled the shore team. A shallow local tender approached from the landing. Its crew sounded the short approach anew and agreed a reduced load. Two passengers transferred first, then the third. Bot remained aboard the rescue boat; the tender's margin did not stretch to include him.

At the landing, shore workers checked the boarding height against the day's water. They assisted each passenger up the short dock stair, along the connector and through the four flights to the high path. Between flights the tired passengers rested on the measured landings. A worker stayed with them all the way across the arch and along the north ledge to the refuge. No one climbed through the nesting pocket.

The pilots secured the disabled boat for later recovery. Its cargo would miss the market. The fittings Bot had left ashore would miss their delivery too. Everyone was accounted for, which was a good ending to the rescue and an inconvenient beginning to tomorrow.

Back at the quay, Namu spread out the corridor copy. They entered the new sounding as a local warning awaiting survey, not a permanent change to the entire seabed. Beside it they wrote Bot's name and the measurement method.

“You can keep that correction,” they said.

“And the permitted corridor?”

“Until its next inspection. The date belongs on every copy.”

Bot showed them his record. It contained the time, the corrected approach, the loading decision and the reason for closure. No hidden shore had appeared in the margins.

“I thought you needed everything,” Namu said.

“I thought you were refusing anything.”

They sat with the two statements for a while. From the workshop came an uneven little tune: someone testing an instrument made from a naturally empty shell. Bot listened without trying to improve it.

Namu rolled up the master chart. The limited copy stayed between them, useful and unfinished, with a clear place for the next person's observation.
